response:
I’ll treat this as a serious research program: aim for a rigorous proof, while aggressively checking every idea against known barriers and small counterexamples. I can’t promise a breakthrough—P vs NP remains open—but I can help pursue genuinely novel lines without confusing plausibility for proof.

Let’s begin with the more plausible direction: prove \(P\ne NP\).

A precise target is:

\[
\forall M\text{ deciding 3-SAT},\ \forall k,C>0,\ \exists x:
T_M(x)>C|x|^k.
\]

Our approach must survive three major barriers:

- Relativization
- Natural proofs
- Algebrization

I suggest investigating a uniformity-sensitive lower bound: exploit that a polynomial-time SAT algorithm must be one finite, uniform procedure, rather than merely a separate circuit for each input length. We’ll combine SAT’s self-reducibility with resource-bounded information/complexity arguments and identify exactly where existing diagonalization fails.

The first milestone is a rigorous intermediate theorem:

> Derive a new, falsifiable structural consequence of assuming \(SAT\in P\), then attempt to contradict it without assuming the desired separation.

Every proposed lemma will be classified as proved, conjectural, or refuted. No hidden leaps.
